events.reason: Short of breath on exertion, more nosebleeds

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: Exertional dyspnea, recurrent epistaxis, father with pulmonary AVMs

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
41F. Says the stairs to her classroom (third floor) have her winded this winter in a way they didn't last year, has to stop on the landing. No chest pain, no cough, no wheeze, no orthopnea or leg swelling, no palpitations or near-syncope. Nosebleeds more often since the heat came on, 2-3 a week, usually 10 min, one last week closer to 30. No blood in stool. Periods still heavy.

Reminds me her father was told he had AVMs in the lungs. She doesn't know details.

Meds unchanged. Iron at bedtime.

Exam: pale. No respiratory distress at rest. Nares: dried blood L anterior septum, nothing active. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear throughout. No clubbing. No edema. Calves soft.

A/P:
1. Exertional dyspnea - anemia the obvious candidate, but with her father's lung AVMs and her nosebleeds I want pulmonary to look at her for an AVM/shunt. Referral placed.
2. Iron deficiency anemia - CBC, iron studies today.
3. Recurrent epistaxis - humidifier, saline gel to the septum nightly; pressure technique reviewed.
Call/ED for chest pain, fainting, a nosebleed that won't stop with 20 minutes of pressure.

documents.title: Results and referral
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Paula - your hemoglobin dropped to 9.7, lower than last year, and your iron is very low. That likely explains a good part of the breathlessness on the stairs. Keep the iron going every day. The pulmonology referral is in; their office will call you. Please bring a list of what you know about your father's diagnosis if you can get it from him.

documents.title: RE: Results and referral
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you. I called my dad, he says they called it a hereditary thing with blood vessels and he had something done to the lung ones years ago. My aunt has the nosebleeds too. Pulm called, I'm in March 17.

events.reason: Dyspnea on exertion and recurrent epistaxis

conditions.label: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
conditions.note: Curacao criteria: epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, affected first-degree relative

reports.text: Indication: exertional dyspnea, suspected hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; evaluate for intrapulmonary shunt. Technically adequate study. Normal left ventricular size and wall thickness. Left ventricular ejection fraction 72% by biplane method, high normal, with no regional wall motion abnormality. Normal right ventricular size and function. Atria normal in size. Aortic, mitral, tricuspid and pulmonic valves structurally normal without stenosis or regurgitation. Estimated right ventricular systolic pressure normal. No pericardial effusion. Agitated saline injected via left antecubital vein at rest and with Valsalva release: no bubbles seen in the left heart at any cycle.
reports.conclusion: High-normal LV systolic function (EF 72%). No valvular abnormality. Agitated saline contrast study negative for intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 3/9/1979. Seen 3/17/2021 at your request.

Reason: worsening exertional dyspnea and nosebleeds.

History: 42-year-old teacher, never smoker, with nosebleeds dating back to her early teens, cauterized once in her twenties, now more frequent. Over the winter she has become breathless climbing stairs. No cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, migraine-type headaches or neurologic events. Her father carries a diagnosis of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with treated pulmonary AVMs, and a paternal aunt has the same nosebleed history. Her husband's side has nothing similar. She and her husband are concerned about her son, now 13, and whether he could have inherited this.

Medications: carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 TID (neurology), ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with vitamin C, loratadine as needed.
Allergies: no drug allergies; shellfish (hives); environmental.

Examination: comfortable at rest, SpO2 98% on room air. Several small red telangiectasias on the lower lip and tongue tip and on the pads of two fingers on the right hand, blanching. Nasal septum with crusting. Lungs clear; no bruit over the chest. Heart regular, no murmur. No clubbing or cyanosis.

Data: labs from your office and ours show iron deficiency anemia, hemoglobin in the 9s with microcytosis. Transthoracic echo with bubble study today: EF 72%, valves normal, no shunt.

Assessment: she meets three of the four Curacao criteria (spontaneous recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias at characteristic sites, a first-degree relative with HHT), which makes the diagnosis of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia definite. I explained that HHT is autosomal dominant and arises from defects in the TGF-beta signaling pathway in blood vessel walls, so each of her children has a 50% chance of inheriting it. The negative bubble study makes a clinically significant pulmonary AVM unlikely, and I attribute her exertional dyspnea to the iron deficiency anemia, which in turn is fed by both her heavy menses and the nosebleeds.

Recommendations: continue iron replacement through your office; nasal humidification as you started. Return to us for new respiratory symptoms.

Thank you for the referral.
Pulmonology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after pulm. Letter reviewed: definite HHT by Curacao criteria (epistaxis, lip/tongue/finger telangiectasias, father affected). Bubble echo negative, EF 72%, no valve disease; dyspnea attributed to anemia.

She is relieved there's no lung AVM and a little shaken by the name. Lots of questions about her son. We talked about what the diagnosis means day to day for her (nosebleeds, iron) and that the pediatrician is the right person to start with for him.

Still winded on stairs. Nosebleeds a bit better with the humidifier.

A/P:
- HHT - added to problem list.
- Iron deficiency anemia - on daily oral iron, fed by menses + epistaxis. Continue. CBC at the physical.
- PD - per neuro.
RTC fall.

documents.title: Immunization registry update
documents.author: MA
documents.body: State registry reconciliation: COVID-19 Pfizer-BioNTech dose 1 04/06/2021 and dose 2 04/27/2021 given at a community pharmacy. Added to immunization history. Primary series complete.

documents.title: Saline gel
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Is it ok to keep using the saline gel all summer even though the air isn't dry? The nosebleeds are down to maybe one a week. School's out in 2 weeks, yay.

documents.title: RE: Saline gel
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Yes, keep it up year round, it helps protect the fragile vessels in the nose. Glad they're less frequent. Enjoy the break!

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
42F annual. Full in-person classes again. Feels a bit better than last winter on the stairs, not back to normal. Nosebleeds roughly weekly, short. Periods heavy as ever. Son started 8th grade.

Meds: carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 TID, ferrous sulfate 325 daily, loratadine prn. Allergies unchanged.
PHQ-2 0. Never smoker, wine 1-2/wk.

Exam: NAD. Telangiectasias lower lip, tongue tip. Thyroid nl. RRR. Lungs clear. Abd soft. No edema. Neuro nonfocal, no tremor.

A/P:
- HHT / IDA: CBC, ferritin today. Continue oral iron, saline gel, humidifier.
- PD: neuro follow-up due; she'll call them.
- HM: mammogram ordered. Flu shot at nurse visit in Oct. COVID primary series done in April.
RTC 1 yr.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hemoglobin 10.4, a little better than February, iron stores still low. Kidney and liver tests normal. Stay with the daily iron; we'll keep watching.

documents.title: Immunization
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Influenza quadrivalent 0.5 mL IM L deltoid. Afebrile, no prior reactions. VIS given. Observed 15 min, no issues.

reports.text: Bilateral CC and MLO views with tomosynthesis. Comparison 10/2020 and 10/2019. Heterogeneously dense. No suspicious mass, calcification or distortion. No change.

conditions.label: Insomnia
conditions.note: Sleep-onset insomnia driven by restless legs

documents.title: Neurology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 03/14/2022.

Paula, 43, whom we follow for Parkinson disease and who was diagnosed with HHT by pulmonology last year, came back to clinic, a little overdue for her annual visit, mainly because of poor sleep.

For roughly the past year, once she lies down at night she gets a deep, unpleasant ache in both calves with an overwhelming need to move her legs. Getting up and walking eases it, and she often paces her bedroom several times before she can fall asleep. It happens only in the evening and at night when she is still; standing, sitting through the school day and daytime are free of it. She is tired every day from the lost sleep. She has no history of anxiety, depression or any other psychiatric problem. Parkinson symptoms remain well controlled on carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily.

She eats a vegetarian diet. Menses are regular but heavy. She remains on oral iron for long-standing iron deficiency.

Examination on medication: neurologic examination normal, including mental status, cranial nerves, strength, tone, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. No tremor or bradykinesia.

Impression:
1. Restless legs syndrome, meeting all essential criteria, with chronic insomnia as its consequence. Iron deficiency is the most likely driver here.
2. Parkinson disease, stable.

We discussed management. The first step is iron: her ferritin should be checked, and the goal in RLS is a ferritin above 75, well above the usual lower limit. Please check iron studies and consider whether she can reach that orally. Regular sleep and wake times, moderate exercise earlier in the day, cutting back on evening wine and caffeine, and avoiding sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine at night (her loratadine is fine). We also talked about what this means long term: RLS is usually chronic and can slowly become more frequent, and dopaminergic medicines used for it can over time worsen it (augmentation), which is one reason we are not adding anything today. No change to her carbidopa-levodopa.

Follow-up in 12 months.
Outside neurology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here to go over neuro's letter. Dx restless legs, with insomnia from it. Neuro wants ferritin >75.

She says nights are the worst part of her life right now: legs start up around 10, pacing, asleep maybe by midnight-1, up at 5:45 for school. Not napping. No snoring per husband. Mood ok, frustrated.

Taking ferrous sulfate daily at bedtime with vit C, 2 h from levodopa, misses maybe one dose a week. Some constipation.

Exam: pale, otherwise unremarkable. Legs normal.

A/P:
- RLS / insomnia: iron studies + CBC today. Sleep measures per neuro reviewed; she's cutting the evening glass of wine.
- IDA: if ferritin still very low, she would prefer to keep trying oral before anything IV. Try alternate-day dosing if constipation is limiting.
- HHT, PD stable.

documents.title: Iron results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Ferritin came back at about 10, so a long way from the target of 75 neurology mentioned, and hemoglobin is about where it was in the fall. Let's give the oral iron a fair shot with very consistent daily dosing for the next few months and recheck at your physical. If it isn't moving we can talk about other options.

documents.title: Missed appointment
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: LM for pt re: missed 6/14 follow-up. Pt called back: last week of school, graduation duties, forgot. Doing about the same. Prefers to wait for her fall physical. Offered sooner; declined. Physical booked 9/20.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
43F annual. RLS: some nights better, still paces 2-3 nights a week. Sleep 5-6 h on school nights. Cut evening wine to weekends. Nosebleeds weekly, short. Heavy periods. Took iron most days over the summer.

Meds: carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 TID; ferrous sulfate 325 daily; loratadine prn.
Allergies: NKDA; shellfish; tree pollen/dust mites.
FHx: father HHT; mother hypothyroid + GAD; son ADHD.
PHQ-2 1.

Exam: NAD. Lip and tongue telangiectasias. Thyroid normal. RRR, lungs clear. Abd soft. Skin ok. Neuro nonfocal.

A/P:
- IDA/HHT: CBC, ferritin. Continue oral iron.
- RLS/insomnia: sleep habits; neuro f/u in spring.
- HM: lipids, TSH (mother hypothyroid) today. Mammogram ordered. Flu and bivalent COVID booster at nurse visit 10/4. Pap due next year.
RTC 1 yr.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Paula, cholesterol and thyroid are normal. Hemoglobin and ferritin are essentially unchanged from the spring, still low. Keep going with the iron and we'll recheck in the spring.

documents.title: Immunization
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Flu (L deltoid) and bivalent Pfizer COVID booster (R deltoid) given IM. Screening negative. VIS/EUA fact sheet given. Observed 15 min. No reaction.

reports.text: Bilateral digital mammogram with tomosynthesis compared to 2019-2021. Heterogeneously dense tissue. No suspicious findings.
